THOUGHT: The patient is a teen with a long history of ALL and two prior CNS relapses who now has a 3‑month history of progressive bilateral proptosis, blurred vision and chronic frontal headache. Examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling (papilledema), symmetric exophthalmos (Hertel 25 mm OU), normal eye movements and IOP, and only mildly reduced acuity. The CSF opening pressure is massively elevated (65.5 cm H2O) and the CSF contains a very high blast count (1,400 × 10^6/L). Neuroimaging demonstrates progressive bony remodeling (scalloping) of the orbital roof/floor and lateral displacement of the medial orbital walls — changes consistent with a chronic expansile process or long‑standing raised intracranial pressure causing bone remodeling. Taken together the most parsimonious diagnosis is recurrent ALL with leptomeningeal (neoplastic) infiltration producing markedly raised intracranial pressure (leukemic meningitis) with secondary bilateral papilledema and resultant apparent globe protrusion. Alternative possibilities include direct orbital leukemic infiltration (chloromas/granulocytic sarcoma) causing proptosis, but the presence of CSF blasts and very high opening pressure point to leptomeningeal disease as the primary process. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, thyroid orbitopathy, cavernous sinus disease or other intracranial/ orbital masses are less likely given the positive CSF cytology and oncologic history, but remain reasonable differentials to consider if additional data altered the picture.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Leukaemic leptomeningeal (CNS) relapse / neoplastic meningitis from ALL causing markedly raised intracranial pressure with bilateral papilledema and secondary proptosis
2) Direct orbital leukemic infiltration (bilateral orbital chloromas / granulocytic sarcoma) producing proptosis ± optic nerve compromise
3) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) with papilledema and mild globe protrusion (less likely due to CSF blasts and leukemia history)
4) Thyroid-associated orbitopathy (Graves disease) causing bilateral proptosis and optic neuropathy (less likely given normal motility/clinical context)
5) Intracranial/orbital mass (eg, meningioma, mucocele, chronic expansile lesion causing bony remodeling) or cavernous sinus pathology (eg, thrombosis) producing raised ICP/proptosis (less likely given CSF findings and clinical course)
